deckTitle: George's Ideology-Wrestling Kayfabizarro Komik Kards — A Field Guide to the War for Your Mind (Version 4.1 Unstable)

cards.power: Shadow Play: Force another player to accept your description of a card as truth until end of turn.
cards.lore: Myth solved the coordination problem. Tell them a story about where they came from, make it sacred, and make questioning it dangerous.
cards.gradeReason: Forcing a player to accept your description of a card as truth is performative reality-construction — the first ideological move in the deck made literal.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: cave painting. Subject: bear casting a monstrous shadow, two small figures accepting it as the whole truth. Mood: administered belief.

cards.power: In-Group Bias: Discard a card to ignore any effect from a player not in your 'alliance'.
cards.lore: The tribe is the first state. Its ideology is simple: In-group is sacred; Out-group is profane. We don't need a reason to discriminate.
cards.gradeReason: Alliance-filtering is mechanically correct but its cost (discard) softens what should be a free and automatic reflex.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: night camp illustration. Subject: wolf pack howling at the moon, firelight ending exactly where the darkness begins. Mood: enforced boundary.

cards.power: Gatekeeper: You interpret the dice roll. Change a [1] to a [5] or vice versa once per game.
cards.lore: The first ideological professional. He mediates between the human and the divine. He controls the narrative, so he controls the tribe.
cards.gradeReason: Permanent die-result interpretation — used exactly once, saved for the right moment — is the Shaman's power distilled to one irrevocable action.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: shamanic vision art. Subject: owl with antlers holding a glowing die, the number on the face shifting as it watches. Mood: authorized interpretation.

cards.power: Social Death: Ban a specific word. Anyone who says it loses a card.
cards.lore: The original cancellation. Not a law, but a boundary. Cross it, and you threaten the fabric of reality itself.
cards.gradeReason: Banning a word in a storytelling game is linguistic kayfabe — the table will immediately try to say the word, which is the point.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: warning sign woodcut. Subject: porcupine inside a red X, surrounding words erased, a single forbidden syllable visible at the edge. Mood: enforced silence.

cards.power: God-King: Your commands are natural law. Re-roll any die result that displeases you.
cards.lore: Not a metaphor. A governance technology. His will is indistinguishable from the movement of the sun.
cards.gradeReason: Unlimited die-displeasure veto is the God-King mechanic — the table cannot stop a result the Pharaoh finds inconvenient.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Egyptian fresco parody. Subject: lion pharaoh on a throne, pointing at a die and raising one eyebrow. Mood: celestial indifference.

cards.power: Written in Stone: Lock a Scene card. It cannot be moved, changed, or covered for 2 turns.
cards.lore: The political made sacred. Don't question the law, because the sun god wrote it. The first "Terms of Service".
cards.gradeReason: Scene-locking for 2 turns is structurally useful but "First Terms of Service" is the deck's best parenthetical and the power doesn't match its wit.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ancient legal monument. Subject: ram carving rules onto a stone slab, a beetle watching from the corner. Mood: precedent set.

cards.power: Mediator: Look at the top 3 cards of the deck. Arrange them in the order that benefits you.
cards.lore: Knowledge/Power. The priests read the stars and interpret the gods. The first bureaucracy of meaning.
cards.gradeReason: Arranging the next three cards for personal benefit is priestly power made structural — the future is now administered.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: temple astronomical diagram. Subject: vulture in priestly robes adjusting a celestial map, constellation order changing. Mood: curated providence.

cards.power: Blame Shifting: Transfer a negative effect from yourself to another player.
cards.lore: Culture is a death-denial system. We need stories to be eternal. When they fail, we need someone to bleed for it.
cards.gradeReason: Effect transfer is clean and correct but the Girard reference in the lore is richer than the mechanic — "bleed for it" wants a cost attached.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ritual procession illustration. Subject: goat loaded with bags labeled SINS walking through a gate into the desert, crowd relieved behind it. Mood: collective relief at someone else's expense.

cards.power: "The Question: Demolish a player's Story by asking 'Define your terms.' They must discard a card."
cards.lore: "He didn't deliver a system; he demolished them. Epistemological sabotage has consequences. Usually execution."
cards.gradeReason: "Define your terms" as a card power is epistemological sabotage made playable — three words that will end any weak argument at any table.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Greek court illustration. Subject: bee interrogating a horse mid-sentence, the horse already reaching for a discard pile. Mood: forensic inconvenience.

cards.power: "Noble Lie: Swap a card on the Stage with a card from your hand. Claim it was always there."
cards.lore: "The first totalitarian utopia. Rulers who know the Truth, and noble lies told to the masses for their own good."
cards.gradeReason: Physically replacing a Stage card and claiming it was always there is the Noble Lie enacted at the table — the table will believe it or won't, and both outcomes are correct.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: shadow theatre. Subject: moles watching shadows on a cave wall, the object casting them replaced mid-shadow by something different. Mood: managed reality.

cards.power: Inner Citadel: Ignore one event that would destroy your Actor. Duty is freedom.
cards.lore: "Philosophy for ruling classes who don't want to be questioned. Focus on your Inner life; accept your station."
cards.gradeReason: Single-use Actor protection is mechanically solid but the lore's class-analysis barb is the more dangerous idea — the power lets you ignore consequence rather than wrestle it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: storm illustration. Subject: stone turtle meditating in a lightning storm, waves hitting the base, expression unchanged. Mood: practiced indifference.

cards.power: Rhetoric: You may lie about your card's stats. If no one calls Blödsinn, the lie becomes true.
cards.lore: "Man is the measure of all things. Truth is just what you can convince people of. The first political consultants."
cards.gradeReason: Lying about your card's stats until the table accepts it is the Sophist argument made operational — the table's credulity is the only mechanic that matters.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: marketplace debate. Subject: chameleon in a toga holding a bottle labeled TRUTH SERUM and SNAKE OIL simultaneously. Mood: performative certainty.

cards.power: Monopoly on Meaning: Cancel another player's move. Cite "God's Will."
cards.lore: Kings are kings by grace. To question hierarchy is to question reality. A monopoly is efficient until it isn't.
cards.gradeReason: Canceling by citing God's Will is theatrically correct but structurally it's a veto — the "cite God's Will" clause needs to be said aloud to work.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: heraldic parody. Subject: peacock on a dunghill wearing a crown, rays of light coming from behind it, village below not questioning this. Mood: legitimized absurdity.

cards.power: Purge: Force a player to reveal their hand. Discard any card that contradicts your current Quest.
cards.lore: Ideology enforcement at its most literal. The template for every thought-policing system to follow.
cards.gradeReason: Revealing a hand and purging contradictions is the Inquisition mechanic with no theatrical distance — the player's hand is now a doctrinal audit.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: medieval horror. Subject: spider in a mitre examining playing cards on a web, burning any that don't match. Mood: doctrinal compliance.

cards.power: Internalized Guilt: All other players must discard 1 card at random. We are all fallen.
cards.lore: Political authority is necessary because you are broken. Legitimizes the state while telling you you deserve it.
cards.gradeReason: Mass random discard justified by "we are all fallen" is the Original Sin mechanic — everyone pays for a state they didn't create and didn't choose.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: baroque religious parody. Subject: serpent eating itself, coin collection box visible in the corner, everyone putting something in. Mood: universal liability.

cards.power: Labor: Generate +1 to the Quest Die. You receive no credit.
cards.lore: Natural order. Some animals are naturally suited to labor. The great biologization of hierarchy.
cards.gradeReason: +1 to Quest Die with no credit is the correct concept but it's a number adjustment — the absence of credit needs to be visible at the table, not just implied by the card.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: feudal labor illustration. Subject: donkey pulling a full cart toward a castle, a carrot dangling ahead, scoreboard showing zero. Mood: productive invisibility.

cards.power: "Viral Load: Draw 3 cards. Distribute them to other players. They cannot refuse."
cards.lore: "Destroyed the information monopoly. An epistemological revolution. Now anyone can interpret the source code."
cards.gradeReason: Forcing cards onto other players who cannot refuse is the printing press mechanic — information spreads whether the recipient wants it or not.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: workshop chaos. Subject: yellow rabbit at a press, pages flying into every player's area simultaneously, ink everywhere. Mood: uncontrolled distribution.

cards.power: "Realpolitik: Steal a card from another player. Justify it as 'necessary for stability.'"
cards.lore: "He didn't invent the game; he just printed the rules. Be a lion and a fox. Morality is instrumental."
cards.gradeReason: The justification clause — "necessary for stability" — must be spoken aloud, which makes the theft a performance rather than a mechanic.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Renaissance court portrait. Subject: fox in doublet holding a rose in one hand and a knife behind its back, expression entirely sincere. Mood: instrumental grace.

cards.power: "Schism: Split the Quest Die into two separate dice. The narrative now has two conflicting goals."
cards.lore: "Sola Scriptura. You don't need a priest. Democratization of meaning is also fragmentation of meaning."
cards.gradeReason: Splitting one Quest Die into two conflicting goals is the Reformation mechanic — the game now has a schism and the table must negotiate which goal governs.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Reformation woodcut. Subject: bull nailing a document to a door, the door cracking into two separate paths. Mood: principled fissure.

cards.power: "Self-Determination: Change the suit/type of your Actor card. You can become whatever you choose."
cards.lore: "Man at the center. No fixed nature. We are not waiting for heaven; we are building it here."
cards.gradeReason: Actor type-change is strong but suit/type needs definition in the game context — the freedom the card promises is bounded by the same ambiguity.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Renaissance self-portrait parody. Subject: chimpanzee looking into a mirror and seeing a different animal each time. Mood: contingent selfhood.

cards.power: "The Terror: Remove the Actor with the highest stats from the game. For the General Will."
cards.lore: "When ideological purity meets power. Robespierre thought he knew the General Will. Then it ate him."
cards.gradeReason: Removing the highest-stats Actor "For the General Will" is the Terror in one clause — ideological purification that always finds one more enemy at the top.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: revolutionary horror. Subject: praying mantis in a tricolor cockade, a head in a basket below, the crowd already pointing at the next highest card. Mood: self-consuming virtue.

cards.power: "Consent: Negate an action unless all players vote to allow it."
cards.lore: "Man is born free, but lives in chains. Legitimate government is a deal. But who signed it?"
cards.gradeReason: Unanimous consent to proceed is the most paralyzing legitimate mechanic in the deck — one dissenter stops everything, which is both the promise and the problem of the social contract.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Enlightenment legal illustration. Subject: beaver with quill and chains, signing a document while standing in a fence. Mood: negotiated constraint.

cards.power: "Categorical Imperative: Establish a rule (e.g., 'No blue cards'). It applies to everyone, including you."
cards.lore: "Reason is universal. Ideology as engineering. Just don't ask who gets excluded from 'Reason'."
cards.gradeReason: A self-binding universal rule is the Categorical Imperative at the table — the card's credibility depends on whether the player actually follows the rule they set.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: steampunk mechanism. Subject: mechanical bird assembling a universal law from gears, one gear labeled EXCEPTION already removed. Mood: systematic self-entrapment.

cards.power: "Natural Rights: You cannot be targeted by 'State' or 'Group' effects this turn."
cards.lore: "Life, Liberty, Property. Existed before the state. The foundation of the modern 'User Interface'."
cards.gradeReason: State/Group immunity is mechanically clean but "User Interface" is the lore's best word and the power ignores it — the card should cost something to enact the individualism it advertises.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: libertarian illustration parody. Subject: cat on an iron fence, looking down at the common ground below with visible disdain. Mood: opted out.

cards.power: "Market Forces: Swap the positions of any two cards on the Stage. Claim it happened naturally."
cards.lore: "No central planner needed. Self-interest yields collective welfare. A beautiful myth for the winners."
cards.gradeReason: "Claim it happened naturally" is the invisible hand made audible — the player must perform the myth's self-justification out loud.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ghost economics illustration. Subject: translucent octopus rearranging chess pieces, an arrow pointing to the new position labeled NATURAL OUTCOME. Mood: deniable agency.

cards.power: "Efficiency: Discard 2 cards to draw 3. Maximize throughput."
cards.lore: "Alienation as infrastructure. Workers separated from the product, the process, and themselves."
cards.gradeReason: Net-positive card trade is mechanically efficient and correctly named but it produces no theatre — you optimize silently, which is accurate and disappointing simultaneously.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: industrial engraving. Subject: ant operating a machine that converts ants into gears, the output used to buy more ants. Mood: productive self-erasure.

cards.power: "Legal Fiction: Treat this card as a Player. It has rights but no body to punish."
cards.lore: "A legal person with no soul to save and no body to incarcerate. The dominant species of the modern era."
cards.gradeReason: Treating a card as a Player with rights is the corporate personhood mechanic — the table now has an entity that plays but cannot be held accountable.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: legal satire. Subject: blue whale in a briefcase at the table, no one able to reach it despite everything happening around it. Mood: structural invulnerability.

cards.power: "Rational Self-Interest: Take a card from the discard pile if it helps you immediately."
cards.lore: "The utility-maximizing agent. A lonely, sociopathic model of human nature that we decided to become."
cards.gradeReason: Discard-pile retrieval for immediate benefit is the most generic utility mechanic in the deck — the lore's "we decided to become" is the most disturbing line on the page and the power doesn't honor it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: economic satire diagram. Subject: squirrel buried in acorns with an abacus, calculating, alone, surrounded by labeled utility curves. Mood: optimized isolation.

cards.power: "Historical Materialism: Flip the Quest Die to its opposite face (1 becomes 6). Invert the power structure."
cards.lore: "He changed the questions. History is class struggle. But he didn't solve the problem of power."
cards.gradeReason: Flipping the die to its opposite face is the most structurally honest mechanic in the deck — the inversion is total, immediate, and creates a new problem the lore already names.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: revolutionary woodcut. Subject: beaver at a writing desk, die on the table showing 1, the shadow behind it showing 6. Mood: diagnosed contradiction.

cards.power: "Dictatorship of the Proletariat: You make decisions for another player this turn. They 'don't know what's good for them.'"
cards.lore: "The workers need professionals to lead them. The path from liberation to the Gulag is paved with 'consciousness'."
cards.gradeReason: Playing another player's turn "because they don't know what's good for them" is the Vanguard mechanic — the quotes around consciousness are doing load-bearing ideological work.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Soviet propaganda parody. Subject: wolf in a red armband making decisions for a row of badgers who are looking at each other uncertainly. Mood: administered liberation.

cards.power: "Seize the Means: Take control of a 'Tool' or 'Location' card on the Stage."
cards.lore: "The weapon of the producer. When the machine stops, you see who really runs it."
cards.gradeReason: Taking control of a Tool or Location is correct but requires those card types to be in play — its power depends on the Stage's contents rather than enacting anything itself.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: labor poster. Subject: badgers with arms crossed in front of a stopped factory, a clock on the wall showing who's actually needed. Mood: withheld productivity.

cards.power: "Estrangement: A player cannot use their Actor's special ability this turn. They are separated from their potential."
cards.lore: "Separated from your labor, your product, your humanity. The engine of the system is your unhappiness."
cards.gradeReason: Blocking an Actor ability for one turn is a standard debuff — "separated from their potential" promises something more existential than a one-turn lockout delivers.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: caged bird illustration. Subject: bluebird in a cage with a painting of sky on the wall, special ability text crossed out with a single line. Mood: structural estrangement.

cards.power: "No Masters: Remove a 'Leader' or 'Authority' card from play."
cards.lore: "Property is theft. Domination is the enemy. Order without power."
cards.gradeReason: Authority-removal is correct and needed but depends on Leader/Authority cards existing — it is reactive by nature rather than generative.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: anarchist illustration. Subject: black cat atop a rubble pile, anarchist flag above, looking distinctly unbossed. Mood: structural vacancy.

cards.power: "Cooperation: Give a card from your hand to another player. Both of you draw 1 card."
cards.lore: "Evolution is not just competition. Kropotkin was right: we survived because we helped each other."
cards.gradeReason: Net positive for both players through voluntary exchange is the only card in this ideological arc whose mechanic produces more than it costs — the table feels the difference.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: naturalist illustration. Subject: two bees exchanging pollen, both growing larger from the transfer, the hive visible as a background. Mood: mutual surplus.

cards.power: "Direct Action: Destroy a Scene card immediately. No voting."
cards.lore: "Propaganda of the deed. Sometimes you don't debate the wall; you blow it up."
cards.gradeReason: "No voting" is the anarchist doctrine made table mechanic — The Social Contract requires unanimous consent; The Molotov requires none.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: direct action illustration. Subject: bombardier beetle hitting a brick wall — the wall mid-explosion, no committee visible. Mood: decisive detonation.

cards.power: "Prefigurative Politics: Create a 'Safe Zone' where cards cannot be attacked or removed."
cards.lore: "Build the new society in the shell of the old. The means must embody the ends."
cards.gradeReason: Protective zone creation is mechanically useful but passive — the commune protects rather than builds, which is thematically incomplete.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: self-organized settlement. Subject: meerkats building a shared space inside the ruins of a larger structure, the outer walls still crumbling. Mood: interior construction.

cards.power: "Rally Round: Gain +1 Power for every card of the same 'suit' or color in play."
cards.lore: "The totem object. Ideology made material. People die for the colored cloth."
cards.gradeReason: Suit-stacking bonus is a competent tribal power but requires same-suit cards to be assembled first — the flag only works if the army already exists.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: nationalist parody. Subject: bison charging with a red cape attached, every animal of the same color falling into formation behind it. Mood: rallied momentum.

cards.power: "Exclusion: Prevent a new card from entering the Stage this turn."
cards.lore: "Imagined lines enforced by real guns. Defining who belongs by who doesn't."
cards.gradeReason: Preventing Stage entry is clean and correct — "imagined lines enforced by real guns" is a better card than its mechanic, but the mechanic does what it says.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: surveillance landscape. Subject: German shepherd patrolling a line drawn in sand, a map in the background showing the line was moved last week. Mood: enforced cartography.

cards.power: "My Country Right or Wrong: Ignore a logic error or 'Blödsinn' call if it favors you."
cards.lore: "Benedict Anderson called it an 'Imagined Community.' You will never meet them, but you will kill for them."
cards.gradeReason: Immunity to a Blödsinn call if it favors you is the precise mechanic of motivated patriotic reasoning — the flag exempts you from epistemology this turn.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: eagle patriotic parody. Subject: bald eagle with VR goggles displaying only flags, a logic error visible just outside the frame. Mood: selective truth.

cards.power: "Extraction: Take a card from another player's hand. Keep it."
cards.lore: "Imperial nationalism. We are so superior we have a duty to rule you and take your stuff."
cards.gradeReason: Hand theft is correctly named and blunt but it's a standard mechanic — "a duty to rule you and take your stuff" is more devastating than the power it sits under.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: natural history parody. Subject: cuckoo bird taking eggs from a smaller bird's nest, calling it civilization. Mood: benevolent appropriation.

cards.power: Panopticon: Play with your hand revealed. You cannot lie.
cards.lore: Surveillance is not just watching; it's modifying. He loves you because he owns your mind.
cards.gradeReason: Playing with your hand permanently revealed is the Panopticon — you cannot lie because the table sees everything, which changes every move you make.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: surveillance horror. Subject: enormous eye with a camera lens inside it, all cards fanned face-up beneath it, the owner unable to bluff. Mood: transparent captivity.

cards.power: Disappear: Place a card in the "Memory Hole" (under the table). It never existed.
cards.lore: The revolution eats its children. Industrialized removal of "inconvenient" reality.
cards.gradeReason: Placing a card under the table so it "never existed" is the best physical theatre instruction in the deck — the card is gone and the table must pretend it was always gone.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Soviet industrial. Subject: polar bear lowering a card through a trapdoor labeled MEMORY HOLE, other cards already not noticing the gap. Mood: industrialized absence.

cards.power: Confession: Force a player to admit they cheated (even if they didn't). They lose a turn.
cards.lore: Reality is contested. You must not just die; you must agree that you deserved it.
cards.gradeReason: Forced confession of cheating — guilty or not — is the Show Trial mechanic at the table; the player loses a turn and must perform their guilt.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: kangaroo court illustration. Subject: kangaroo judge banging a gavel, defendant in the dock already nodding in agreement before the charge is read. Mood: preordained verdict.

cards.power: Cognitive Dissonance: Play two cards that contradict each other. Both take effect.
cards.lore: Holding two contradictory beliefs simultaneously. The ultimate flexibility of the broken mind.
cards.gradeReason: Playing two contradictory cards with simultaneous effect is a table crisis — two truths that cancel each other now both govern the game, which is the point.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: psychological diagram. Subject: two-headed snake facing opposite directions, both sets of eyes focused, both mouths open. Mood: simultaneous conviction.

cards.power: "Privatize: Claim a 'Public' card on the Stage as your personal property."
cards.lore: "The market knows best. Democracy is inefficient. Everything is for sale."
cards.gradeReason: Public card privatization is correct but requires a Public card to exist on the Stage — the fundamentalist needs a commons to enclose.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: underwater corporate. Subject: shark in a suit placing a FOR SALE sign on a reef, other fish watching without legal standing. Mood: justified acquisition.

cards.power: "Expertise: Override a die roll with a 'Technical Correction' (set it to 3)."
cards.lore: "It's not political; it's technical. Leave it to the experts. We are optimizing you."
cards.gradeReason: Setting the die to 3 is the Vagus Nerve problem again — a number adjustment with a label, no performance required. "We are optimizing you" demands more than a reset.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: technocratic office. Subject: owl with a cybernetic eye pointing at a calculator, the political implications listed on a whiteboard marked IRRELEVANT. Mood: apolitical certainty.

cards.power: "Crisis Opportunity: If the Quest Die tips/collapses, draw 2 cards immediately."
cards.lore: "Disaster capitalism. Use the crisis to push through changes that would be impossible in peacetime."
cards.gradeReason: Gaining on collapse — rewarded specifically when things go wrong — makes the Shock Doctrine player the only one who benefits from failure, which the table will notice and resent.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: disaster capitalism illustration. Subject: electric eel in a crisis tank, all other fish panicking, the eel drawing cards while sparks fly. Mood: crisis dividend.

cards.power: "Enclosure: Charge other players a 'fee' (discarding a card) to use the Stage."
cards.lore: "Efficiency means stripping the asset. The commons are just uncaptured value waiting to be eaten."
cards.gradeReason: Gating the Stage behind a discard-toll transforms the shared play space into a revenue stream — the table will pay once and then refuse, which IS the historical dynamic.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: grasshopper enclosure illustration. Subject: locust placing a FOR SALE sign on the Stage area itself, holding a clipboard. Mood: administrative voracity.

cards.power: Echo Chamber: You are immune to arguments (effects) from cards of a different color.
cards.lore: Algorithmic personalization. You don't see reality; you see a mirror designed to keep you angry.
cards.gradeReason: Color-immunity is the filter bubble mechanic but it requires color coding to be a established game convention — without that, the table must invent what "different color" means.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: aquarium diagram. Subject: goldfish and shark in the same bowl, the shark invisible to the goldfish due to a VR headset. Mood: curated blindness.

cards.power: Bait: Force an opponent to attack you instead of the Quest.
cards.lore: Irony as armor. Nothing matters, so I can destroy everything for "Lulz".
cards.gradeReason: Redirecting an attack onto yourself to derail the Quest is trolling as a table mechanic — the game stops advancing because someone made themselves the story.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: digital underworld. Subject: wild boar at a laptop under a bridge, typing with intent, Quest visible on a screen it's not reading. Mood: deliberate derailment.

cards.power: Viral Replication: Copy the effect of the last card played.
cards.lore: Self-replicating cultural unit. Weaponized by the Alt-Right, the Left, and cats. Reality is downstream of the JPEG.
cards.gradeReason: "Reality is downstream of the JPEG" is the best lore line on the page — and copying any card's effect without restriction is the meme's power: it doesn't originate, it spreads.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: viral diagram. Subject: smiley-face virus with spider legs replicating identically across the Stage, original source already unidentifiable. Mood: successful mutation.

cards.power: De-Platform: Remove an Actor card from the game. They are "Unpersoned."
cards.lore: Purity spiral. The in-group purges itself to stay holy. Structural violence or accountability? Yes.
cards.gradeReason: Permanent Actor removal with "Unpersoned" as the label is the Cancel Mob mechanic — the lore's terminal "Yes" is the most honest word in this section.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: social media horror. Subject: piranha school shredding an identity badge, the card owner now outside the frame, the group already closing the gap. Mood: accelerated purity.

cards.power: Data Estraction: Look at every player's hand. Keep one card.
cards.lore: Zuboff's nightmare. Predicting and modifying your behavior for profit. The new resource extraction.
cards.gradeReason: Looking at every hand and keeping one card is the data extraction mechanic — the table becomes a behavioural dataset the moment this card is played.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: data center horror. Subject: bat drawing data streams from sleeping figures, keeping one thread per person, all threads converging into a single server. Mood: ambient extraction.

cards.power: Optimisation: Force a specific outcome on the Quest Die (3 or 4) to maximize engagement.
cards.lore: It doesn't hate you. It just maximises a variable that requires your addiction.
cards.gradeReason: Forcing the Die to 3 or 4 is another number-management power — the lore ("requires your addiction") demands a mechanic that creates dependency, not just a die preset.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: surveillance web. Subject: cybernetic spider at the center of a digital web, all threads leading to a die frozen between 3 and 4. Mood: maximized engagement.

cards.power: Simulacrum. Your card counts as having double value, but it disappears if touched (played on).
cards.lore: A copy without an original. The monetization of the self. Existence as performance.
cards.gradeReason: Double value that evaporates on contact is the influencer mechanic — appearance outperforms reality until someone tests it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: social media parody. Subject: peacock with a selfie stick, its reflection twice the size, the original bird fading as the shot is taken. Mood: performative existence.

cards.power: Distraction: Force a player to skip their turn to "doomscroll."
cards.lore: Attention is the scarce resource. Outrage is the most efficient fuel. We are mining your focus.
cards.gradeReason: Forcing a skip called "doomscroll" is precise — the player loses their turn and draws a card, which is the attention economy trade made mechanical.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: digital horror. Subject: moth irresistibly drawn toward a phone screen, Quest visible behind it, acorns scattered forgotten around it. Mood: mined focus.

cards.power: Upgrade: Add +1 to all your stats. You are no longer purely biological.
cards.lore: Haraway's Manifesto. The boundary is dissolved. Embrace the hybrid. Without innocence.
cards.gradeReason: Stat boost across all three values is strong but "without innocence" is the card's most interesting phrase and the power says nothing about the cost of the upgrade.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: cyber-naturalist illustration. Subject: dog with a laser eye and mechanical legs, the biological and mechanical parts stitched together rather than replaced. Mood: dissolved boundary.

cards.power: Acceleration: Roll the die twice. If doubles, the game ends.
cards.lore: History accelerates beyond prediction. The last invention we will ever make. Hope it likes us.
cards.gradeReason: Rolling twice with a game-ending doubles condition is the Singularity mechanic — every time this card is played the table holds its breath, which is the only accurate response.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: portal physics. Subject: melting clock falling into a digital vortex, a die mid-roll visible, the doubles outcome approaching. Mood: pending finality.

cards.power: Feedback Loop: The pressure on the Quest Die increases by 1 every turn automatically.
cards.lore: The planet is on fire. Arguing about ideology while the house burns is a luxury.
cards.gradeReason: Automatic Die pressure increase every turn is the first truly time-bound mechanic in the deck — the Crisis doesn't wait for you to play another card.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wildfire documentary. Subject: koala on a burning branch, the Die visible in the background ticking upward, ideology cards scattered around. Mood: compounding urgency.

cards.power: Bunker Down: You are immune to "Global" effects. You survive alone.
cards.lore: The fantasy of individual survival. Collapse is just an opportunity to finally use your gear.
cards.gradeReason: Global-effect immunity is a passive protection — "you survive alone" is the entire Prepper critique and the mechanic doesn't enact the loneliness it describes.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: bunker illustration. Subject: cockroach in tactical gear surrounded by supplies, watching the Climate Crisis card tick upward through a periscope. Mood: prepared irrelevance.

cards.power: Governance: If players agree, everyone draws 1 card.
cards.lore: Beyond state and market. Communities can manage resources without tragedy. Ostrom's Law.
cards.gradeReason: Conditional mass draw continues to be the weakest mechanic for the strongest institutional theory in the corpus — Ostrom's actual finding (commons survive with rules, not just consent) should be the mechanic.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: pastoral governance. Subject: sheep and shepherds at a round table, the commons behind them visibly green and growing, no tragedy visible. Mood: managed abundance.

cards.power: Fork: Copy any card in play and modify it. It belongs to everyone.
cards.lore: Information wants to be free. Peer production. The Cathedral vs. The Bazaar.
cards.gradeReason: Copying and modifying any card — with the result belonging to all players — is the only commons mechanic in the deck that actually creates something new rather than redistributing existing resources.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: tech collaboration illustration. Subject: penguin showing blueprints to a crowd, copies being made by everyone simultaneously, all slightly different. Mood: generative sharing.

cards.power: Iteration: Improve a card's stat by +1 permanently.
cards.lore: Better today than yesterday. No revolution, just compounding improvement. The modest revolution.
cards.gradeReason: Permanent +1 to a card stat is functionally useful but the philosophy of incremental betterment deserves a mechanic that compounds rather than nudges once.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: underground growth. Subject: earthworm carefully tending a seedling, measuring its height against yesterday's mark, a very small margin of improvement visible. Mood: sustainable increment.

cards.power: I Don't Know: Cancel a "Truth" claim or Dogma.
cards.lore: Knowing the limits of what you know. The only honest position in a chaotic world. Stay fluffy.
cards.gradeReason: "I Don't Know" as a card name that cancels Truth claims is the most subversive defensive move in the deck — certainty is the attack; not-knowing is the shield.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: cosmic minimalism. Subject: tardigrade floating in space, surrounded by competing certainties it is calmly dissolving, one star marked UNCLEAR. Mood: honest uncertainty.

cards.power: The Joker: Counts as any card. Or destroys any card. You decide.
cards.lore: Professional Reality-Wrestler. Don't trust him. Especially not now.
cards.gradeReason: "Don't trust him. Especially not now." — on a card that can be anything or destroy anything — is the most honest warning the game has ever issued about itself.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: meta-cartoon. Subject: yellow rabbit holding every possible card simultaneously, several already on fire, one becoming a different card mid-hold. Mood: sovereign uncertainty.

cards.power: Cut the Narrative: Physically cut a card in half (or pretend to). The card is destroyed.
cards.lore: The ultimate tool of the collage artist. Deconstruct to reconstruct.
cards.gradeReason: The optional "or pretend to" is the only moment of mercy in a card about permanent destruction — the table will always take the real cut.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: collage mechanic illustration. Subject: robotic scissors mid-cut through a playing card, the two halves already beginning to mean different things. Mood: creative destruction.

cards.power: Nonsense: Play instantly when someone takes the game too seriously. Pause the game. Laugh.
cards.lore: The BS Button. Use liberally.
cards.gradeReason: "The BS Button. Use liberally." is the shortest valid lore in the corpus — and a card that pauses the game for mandatory laughter has zero stats and perfect timing.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: emergency button illustration. Subject: enormous red button with a warning triangle, a hand approaching it, no hesitation in the posture. Mood: principled interruption.

cards.power: Chaos: Roll a die. 1-3: Nothing happens. 4-6: Everything changes (swap all hands).
cards.lore: Chance is the only ruler.
cards.gradeReason: 50% chance of swapping all hands is the most democratically violent mechanic in the deck — the Die knows no ideology, and the lore is exactly three words long.
cards.artworkPrompt:
Style: cosmic chaos. Subject: glowing die covered in runes floating above the table, every card mid-flight in anticipation of the roll. Mood: terminal randomness.

verdict: The most intellectually ambitious deck in the corpus — 68 cards that run the complete argument from The Cave Myth to The AI Singularity without dropping a thread. Each era gets its own mechanic logic: the Shaman interprets the die, Plato swaps a card and claims it was always there, The Gulag places a card under the table where it never existed, The Show Trial forces confession from the innocent, Doublethink plays two contradictions simultaneously. Named weakness: the optimistic final section clusters the deck's weakest powers — the Commons, Protopia, and The Algorithm are Grade 3, because hope is harder to mechanize than power, and this may be structurally correct. Table-ready: YES — but bring a strong host, because this deck will provoke genuine disagreement about which cards are critiques and which are endorsements, and that's the whole point.
blurb: 68 cards mapping the complete history of western ideology — from tribal myth to the attention economy. For anyone who suspects the game was rigged before they arrived at the table.

qa.verdict: The most intellectually ambitious deck in the corpus and the only one with a complete argument: ideology runs from the cave to the algorithm, and the mechanic changes with each era. The Shaman interprets the die; Plato's Cave swaps cards and claims they were always there; The Printing Press forces information into unwilling hands; Doublethink plays two contradictions simultaneously; The Gulag places a card under the table where it never existed; The AI Singularity ends the game if doubles land. These are not metaphors — they are the concepts. The satirical evenhandedness is the deck's structural achievement: it is as hard on The Vanguard Party as on The Inquisition, as accurate about The Cancel Mob as about Colonialism. Weakness: the final pages (Commons, Protopia, The Algorithm) cluster the deck's weakest powers at the close — the optimistic cards consistently underperform the critical ones mechanically, which may be structurally accurate but leaves the session ending on number adjustments instead of theatre. Table-ready: yes, with a strong host — this deck will provoke genuine disagreement about which cards are critiques and which are endorsements, which is precisely the point.

notes:
**The strongest satirical construct in the corpus.** The deck covers the complete history of western ideology in 68 cards — from The Cave Myth (40,000 BCE) through The AI Singularity — and uses historical sequencing as its organizing principle. Each section has its own visual aesthetic (cave art, Egyptian fresco, Greek columns, medieval gothic, Enlightenment engraving, industrial, Soviet, digital neon, tech-green), making this the most visually differentiated deck in the corpus.

**Stat format:** Page 2–3 use doubled stat slots (two values per R/A/F field — possibly min/max or two dice). Pages 12–18 use single numerical stats. The doubling appears on the earliest-era cards (tribal, ancient) and disappears by the Greek period — this may be intentional design signifying historical uncertainty/range in early ideologies. Worth confirming with Georg.

**Blödsinn! stamp on Rumpelstiltskin** equivalent: The BLÖDSINN! callout appears between Socrates and Plato's Cave (page 4) as a decorative text element, not on a card face. No parsing confusion.

**VERSION 4.1 UNSTABLE** stamp on cover suggests active iteration. The deck may be the most actively developed in the corpus — previous versions presumably exist.

**Structural observation — optimistic cards underperform:** The final three pages (Alternatives, Future, Meta) contain the deck's weakest powers and its strongest cards simultaneously. Uncle FrizzleBob, The Kayfabizarro Die, and Epistemic Humility are exceptional; The Commons, Protopia, and The Algorithm are Grade 3. The pattern is consistent across decks: hope is harder to mechanize than power.

**Data Estraction** [sic] on Surveillance Capitalism card (page 15) — appears to be a typo on the printed card. Transcribed verbatim as "Data Estraction" per hard rules.

**Lore attribution note:** Unlike Hilfe Ich Bin Ein Mensch, this deck does not include parenthetical academic references. The concepts are cited by entity name only (Zuboff's nightmare, Ostrom's Law, Haraway's Manifesto, Benedict Anderson). This is a deliberate editorial choice — ideological concepts speak without footnotes.

**CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.** Back page (page 19): "Steal this, but give credit to George. No commercial use or FrizzleBob will bite you."

urgent: The Commons (card 61): The third deck with this card and the third time "conditional mass draw" fails to honor the Ostrom citation. Concrete fix: "Governance: Establish a shared rule for card management. If the rule is followed for 2 turns, all players draw 1 card." The rule-and-consequence IS Ostrom's actual mechanism.

THE ALGORITHM (card 54): Forcing the Die to 3 or 4 is technically correct but theatrically dead. Consider: "Optimisation: Each turn, read aloud one card's stats. The table must respond. They cannot stop." The dependency loop IS the mechanic.

ALIENATION (card 32): One-turn Actor ability lockout is too brief and too passive. Alienation in Marx is structural, not episodic. Consider: "Estrangement: Remove the Actor card from its owner's hand. Place it on the Stage. They can see it but cannot use it."
quickWins: THE SERF (card 16): Add "You receive no credit" to the mechanic itself, not just the lore. Mechanic: "Generate +1 to the Quest Die. Another player names you as responsible for the failure if the Quest collapses."

PROTOPIA (card 63): The "compounding improvement" in the lore suggests iteration over time. Change to: "Iteration: Improve a card's stat by +1. If that card survives 2 more turns, improve by another +1." The compound only triggers with patience.
THE PREPPER (card 60): "You survive alone" needs table embodiment. Add: "You may not help other players this turn. If the Quest collapses, you draw 1 card. No one else does."
niceToHave: THE CORPORATION (card 27): "It has rights but no body to punish" — consider adding: "If The Corporation card is challenged (Blödsinn!), the challenger must first identify who is legally responsible. They cannot. The challenge fails." The accountability problem IS the power.

MUTUAL AID (card 34) vs. THE INVISIBLE HAND (card 25): These two cards represent the central debate of the deck and should be flagged as arch-nemesis pairs — playing one in direct response to the other should have a defined interaction. Currently neither card references the other.
VERSION 4.1 UNSTABLE: The version stamp on the cover suggests prior versions exist. A changelog on the back page (like the CC page in other decks) would help collectors and the SSOT.

marketingText:
Kayfabizarro: IDEOLOGY-WRESTLING – A Field Guide to the War for Your Mind (Free Cut & Play Comic Card Game)

Your skull is occupied territory, and the rent was paid in advance by everyone who ever needed you obedient.

You think your beliefs are yours, picked freely off a clean shelf. They were installed. Forty thousand years of ideology, from the first priest who made questioning the campfire story a sin to the feed that monetizes your outrage by the second, all engineered toward the same quiet outcome: you defending the cage as if you chose the bars. "Common sense" is just the winning side's propaganda after it stopped having to argue.

So you wrestle them. One at a time, out loud, at a table. This is Social Story Wrestling: you draw an ideology, you perform its pitch with a straight face, and the room rules whether anyone still buys it. Sixty-eight cards that run the entire history of the western mind, Cave Myth to AI Singularity, through a single brutal question, who does this story serve.

WHAT'S INSIDE?
- The Ideology-Wrestling Core Deck: 68 High-Res "Print, Cut & Play" Cards, featuring DOUBLETHINK, THE GULAG, and THE SOPHIST.
- The Freestyle Rules: The complete Anti-Rulebook. No complicated math, no stat spreadsheets, just storytelling, dice-driven chaos, and the one law that every card can claim anything, as long as you can sell the pitch before the table boos.
- The Chronological War-Map: nine eras with nine visual aesthetics, cave paint to Soviet poster to tech-green neon, marching from The Tribe and The Cave Myth through Luther v1.0, The Vanguard Party ("That wasn't real communism!"), and Surveillance Capitalism, then thinning out at the top where The Commons and Protopia sit, because hope is always harder to mechanize than power.

WHY "PAY WHAT YOU WANT"?
I'm a physician and artist. I make these because a mind that can name its own programming is a much harder mind to rent. Are you broke? Enter "0" and take it. Use it. Run the whole curriculum at your kitchen table. Want to support the craft? Every dollar goes directly into the time I spend drawing the next cards and breaking the next set of rules.

Choose your reality. Become an Epistemic Outlaw.
"They never conquered your mind. They shipped it pre-installed. Time to jailbreak it."
Stay fluffy. — Uncle FrizzleBob
